what_its_for: Sumatriptan is used to treat migraine headaches in adults. It helps relieve the pain, throbbing, nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound that come with a migraine. It is not used to prevent migraines before they start — it only works once a migraine has already begun.
how_to_take: Sumatriptan comes in several forms: tablets you swallow, a nasal spray you use in your nose, and an injection you give yourself under the skin. Always take it as soon as you notice your migraine starting for the best results. You can take it with or without food. If you use the nasal spray, blow your nose gently first, then spray into one nostril while closing the other. If you use the injection, your doctor or nurse will show you exactly how to give it to yourself. Never take more than your doctor prescribed.
dosing: The usual starting dose for tablets is 25 mg, 50 mg, or 100 mg taken as a single dose. If your headache comes back or does not fully go away after 2 hours, you may take a second dose, but wait at least 2 hours between doses. Do not take more than 200 mg in one day. For the nasal spray, the usual dose is one spray (10 mg or 20 mg) in one nostril. If needed, a second spray can be used after 2 hours, but no more than 40 mg in one day. For the injection, the usual dose is 4 mg or 6 mg under the skin. A second injection may be given after 1 hour if needed, but no more than 12 mg in one day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — your dose may be different.
missed_dose: Sumatriptan is not taken on a regular daily schedule, so there is no 'missed dose' in the usual sense. You only take it when you have a migraine. If you realize you forgot to take it early in your migraine and your symptoms are still present, you can take it as soon as you remember. Never double up doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store sumatriptan tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep them away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Store nasal spray and injections as directed on the package — some forms must be kept at room temperature and away from freezing. Keep all forms of this medication out of reach of children and pets. Do not use after the expiration date on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking sumatriptan within 24 hours of using another triptan medicine (such as rizatriptan or zolmitriptan) or ergotamine-type medicines (such as ergotamine or dihydroergotamine), as this can cause serious side effects. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel drowsy or dizzy after taking sumatriptan. Limit alcohol while taking this medicine, as it can make headaches worse. Do not take more doses than prescribed, as overusing migraine medications can actually cause more frequent headaches (called medication overuse headache or rebound headache).
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: chest pain, tightness, or pressure; pain or tightness in your jaw, neck, or throat; shortness of breath; fast or irregular heartbeat; severe stomach pain; sudden weakness or numbness on one side of your body; slurred speech; vision changes; or a very severe or unusual headache different from your normal migraine. Also contact your doctor if your migraines are not getting better with this medicine, if you need to use it more than 10 days per month, or if you experience any allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling, or trouble breathing.
when_it_works: Sumatriptan usually starts to work within 30 minutes to 1 hour after taking the tablet or nasal spray. The injection tends to work faster, often within 10 to 15 minutes. Many people feel significant relief within 2 hours. If you do not get any relief at all after the first dose, call your doctor before taking more. Remember, this medicine works best when taken at the very first sign of a migraine.
special_populations: Older adults (over 65): Sumatriptan is generally not recommended for older adults because the risk of heart and blood vessel problems is higher with age. Talk to your doctor about safer options. Pregnancy: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. The safety of sumatriptan during pregnancy is not fully established, so your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks with you. Breastfeeding: Small amounts of sumatriptan can pass into breast milk. If you are breastfeeding, talk to your doctor — they may suggest pumping and discarding breast milk for 12 hours after taking a dose. Children: Sumatriptan tablets are not approved for children under 18. Some forms of sumatriptan nasal spray are approved for teens aged 12 and older — ask your doctor. Liver or kidney problems: If you have liver or kidney disease, your doctor may recommend a lower dose or a different medication. Always tell your doctor and pharmacist about all your health conditions and all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take.
